'''Viktor Borisovich Adamsky'''{{efn|Also spelled '''Adamskii'''}} ({{langx|ru|Ви́ктор Бори́сович Ада́мский}}; 30 April 1923 – 14 December 2005) was a Soviet and Russian<!--See MOS:NATIONALITY--> [[Physics|physicist]] known for his work on the former [[Soviet atomic bomb project|Soviet program of nuclear weapons]].<ref name="Центральная городская">{{cite web |title=БиблиоМ » АДАМСКИЙ Виктор Борисович |url=http://bibliom.ru/uchenye-gorodov/sarov/adamskij-viktor-borisovich/ |website=bibliom.ru |publisher=Центральная городская |access-date=8 November 2022}}</ref>

==Biography==
Adamsky was born in [[Kyiv|Kiev]], [[Ukrainian SSR]], [[Soviet Union]], on 30 April 1923.<ref name="Центральная городская" /> He entered in the [[Moscow State University]] but was drafted in the [[Red Army]] and served as a radioman in the [[Battle of Stalingrad]] during the [[Eastern Front (World War II)|Eastern Front]] of the [[World War II]].<ref name="Центральная городская" /> In 1945, he went to attend the Moscow State University and earned [[Specialist degree|specialist]] diploma in physics in 1949-1950.<ref name="Центральная городская" /> He was sent to work in the [[All-Russian Scientific Research Institute of Experimental Physics|VNIIEF]] in Arzamas-16, initially working as an engineer before working as a researcher.  In 1974, Adamsky was successful in defending his thesis in physics and earned his [[Candidate of Sciences]] (Russian equivalent of [[PhD]]) from Moscow State University.<ref name="Центральная городская" />  

Adamsky, a physicist, participated in development of thermonuclear charges, first being involved in the development of [[RDS-37]]— the first Soviet two-stage [[Thermonuclear weapon|thermonuclear device]].<ref name="Центральная городская" />   He worked with  [[Vyacheslav Feodoritov]] in the development of the [[RDS-220]], involved in studies concerning the self-excitation of a thermonuclear reaction occurs at high compressions.<ref name="Центральная городская" />  In his initial career, he knew little of what it was but understood he would be working on the hydrogen bomb; he was put up in a hotel, then a flat and was finally invited to share part of a cottage with [[Igor Tamm]] and [[Yuri Romanov (physicist)|Yuri Romanov]]. He found a collegial spirit amongst his workmates, who were very aware of the importance and personal limitations of their situation.<ref name="Центральная городская" />   His experience in physics was first practised under the direction of [[Yakov Zeldovich]] and [[Andrei Sakharov]].<ref name="Центральная городская" />   Theoretical development of the RDS-220 began in July 1961 with a design team chosen by Sakharov (who had met with premier [[Nikita Khrushchev]] on 10 July). By October a report (authored by Sakharov, Adamsky, [[Yuri Babayev]], {{ill|Yuri Smirnov (physicist)|lt=Yuri Smirnov|ru|Смирнов, Юрий Николаевич (физик)}} and [[Yuri Trutnev (scientist)|Yuri Trutnev]]) including the design proposal and calculations had been completed and sent to the design engineers for construction.<ref name="Центральная городская" />   Under huge political pressure and a strict timetable, the typical mathematical rigour associated with previous nuclear bomb development had been replaced by some omissions and the usage of estimates and approximations. As a result, fellow theoretical physicist [[Evsei Rabinovich]] suggested that the design might not work; Sakharov, Adamsky and Feodoritov argued otherwise, but Sakharov did ask the engineers to make some design changes to improve the level of confidence.<ref name="Sakharov">{{cite book|last=Sakharov|first=Andrei|title=Memoirs|publisher=Hutchinson|pages=215–225|location=London|year=1990}}</ref><ref name="Goncharov">{{cite journal|last=Goncharov|first=G.A.|title=American and Soviet H-bomb development programmes: historical background|journal=Physics-Uspekhi|volume=39|number=10|pages=1033–1044|year=1996|url=https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/library/report/1996/goncharov-h-bomb.pdf|access-date=28 October 2018|doi=10.1070/pu1996v039n10abeh000174|bibcode=1996PhyU...39.1033G}}</ref>

Sakharov once visited Adamsky in his office to show him a short story in English by [[Leo Szilard]] (the nuclear bomb patent-holder who conceived of nuclear chain reactions)  called ''[[My Trial as a War Criminal]]''. Szilard's tale of the aftermath of the usage of [[Weapon of mass destruction|weapons of mass destruction]] affected them strongly. Later, both Sakharov and Adamsky provided warnings about the dangers to humanity of nuclear proliferation and the governments behind it.<ref>{{cite book|last=Nelson|first=Craig|title=The Age of Radiance: The Epic Rise and Dramatic Fall of the Atomic Era|pages=268|publisher=Scribner|location=New York|year=2014}}</ref><ref name="Rhodes">{{cite book|last=Rhodes|first=Richard|title=Dark Sun:The Making of the Hydrogen Bomb|publisher=Simon & Schuster|location=New York|year=2005}}</ref><ref name="Norris">{{cite web|url=https://fas.org/nuke/norris/nuc_09089301c_114.pdf|title=Russian/Soviet Nuclear Warhead Production|last=Norris|first=Dr. Robert Standish|website=fas.org|access-date=5 November 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Cold War History|last=Ruotsila|first=Markku|title=The Cold War as a Phenomenon of the Atomic age (review of Yu N. Smirnov essay)|volume=5|number=2|pages=259–279|year=2005|doi=10.1080/14682740500062143}}</ref><ref name="CWIHP">{{cite journal|journal=Cold War International History Project Bulletin|last1=Adamsky|first1=Viktor|last2=Smirnov|first2=Yuri|title=Moscow's Biggest Bomb:The 50-Megaton Test of October 1961|issue=4|year=1994}}</ref>

Two years after the [[RDS-220]] test, Adamsky made a key proposal in a memorandum which it is believed was used to overcome an impasse a few months later during negotiations leading to the [[Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty]] between the U.S.A., the U.K. and the U.S.S.R. in 1963. As a result of Khruschev's acceptance of Adamsky's proposal (it is not known if he actually read it) the ban was agreed upon in the atmosphere, underwater and outer space.<ref name="Goncharov"/><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Journal of Cold War Studies|title=The 1963 Nuclear Test Ban Treaty - A Missed Opportunity for Détente?|volume=10|number=1|pages=3–25|url=http://www3.nccu.edu.tw/~lorenzo/Mastny%20Test%20Ban%20Treaty.pdf|last=Mastny|first=Vojtech|doi=10.1162/jcws.2008.10.1.3|year=2008|archive-date=7 November 2018|access-date=6 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107010143/http://www3.nccu.edu.tw/~lorenzo/Mastny%20Test%20Ban%20Treaty.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Nekropol">{{cite web|url=http://niznov-nekropol.ucoz.ru/index/adamskij_v_b/0-862|title=Ада́мский В.Б.|website=niznov-necropol.ucos.ru|access-date=4 November 2018|archive-date=7 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181107010159/http://niznov-nekropol.ucoz.ru/index/adamskij_v_b/0-862|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://nuclearweaponarchive.org/Russia/TsarBomba.html|title=Big Ivan, The Tsar Bomba ("King of Bombs")|website=nuclearweaponarchive.org|access-date=4 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="Sakharov"/><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|volume=52|number=6|last1=Khariton|first1=Yuli|last2=Adamskii|first2=Viktor|publisher=Educational Foundation for Nuclear Science, Inc.|last3=Smirnoff|first3=Yuri|title=The Way It Was|pages=53–59|year=1996|doi=10.1080/00963402.1996.11456679|bibcode=1996BuAtS..52f..53K}}</ref> Adamsky is buried in Sarov cemetery.<ref name="Nekropol"/>
